Review every anonymous sample against its supplied app-authored reading guide and brief. Inspect naturalness, grammar, lexical/grammatical load, clear references, narrative continuity and unresolved endings, contextual English definitions, missing useful definitions, redundant notes and Japanese readings when present. Scores 1–5: 1 severe mismatch, 2 material problems, 3 usable with reservations, 4 good, 5 unusually strong. content.title: El que estaba reservado
content.story:
Cuando Inés entró en la tienda, encontró dos bultos sobre el mostrador: uno envuelto en papel azul y otro, más pequeño, sujeto con un cordel. Había encargado una lámpara para su hermana y esperaba recogerla antes de que cerraran.

—Vengo por el paquete de Clara —dijo.

El tendero dejó a un lado una factura.

—Sí, lo tengo reservado. ¿Se lo lleva usted?

—Para eso he venido.

Él acercó el bulto azul. Inés lo levantó apenas y volvió a dejarlo sobre el mostrador.

—Pesa bastante para una lámpara.

—Es que va bien protegido.

La respuesta tenía esa seguridad cortés que vuelve incómoda cualquier objeción. Inés buscó la etiqueta sin deshacer el envoltorio.

—Aquí pone «Clara Vidal».

—Exactamente.

—Mi hermana es Clara Montes.

El tendero retiró la mano del paquete, aunque no llegó a apartarlo.

—Ah. Usted ha dicho que venía por el paquete de Clara.

—Porque lo compré para ella.

Se quedaron mirándose un instante. Inés había dado por sentado que él recordaría el encargo del sábado; el tendero había supuesto que aquella mujer venía a recoger una compra a nombre de Clara Vidal. Ninguno había preguntado qué contenía el paquete. El nombre les había bastado para entenderse mal.

—Entonces este no es suyo —dijo él.

—Eso parece.

A Inés le molestó un poco el «entonces», como si el paquete hubiera dejado de pertenecerle por una rectificación suya y no hubiera sido ajeno desde el principio. Sin embargo, el tendero ya estaba revisando las etiquetas con una expresión menos segura.

—Cuando dijo «de Clara», yo habría entendido lo mismo —añadió ella, para aliviarlo—. No fui muy precisa.

—Y yo ni siquiera le pregunté el apellido.

Le dio la vuelta al bulto pequeño. Bajo el cordel había una tarjeta que decía: «Inés Robles. Lámpara».

—Aquí está. La puse a su nombre porque usted hizo el encargo. ¿Clara es la destinataria del regalo?

—Sí. Yo pago; ella recibe. Aunque, después de esto, quizá convenga escribirlo.

Él soltó una risa breve y buscó un lápiz.

—¿Quiere que añada una tarjeta para su hermana?

Inés apoyó una mano en el paquete correcto. El equívoco estaba aclarado, pero la pregunta la hizo demorarse. Había elegido la lámpara con mucha más facilidad que las palabras que debían acompañarla.

—Sí —dijo al fin—. Pero déjeme pensarlo un momento.

El tendero le acercó una tarjeta en blanco y volvió a sus facturas, esta vez sin dar nada por sentado.

glossary.meaning: A wrapped parcel or bundle whose contents are not immediately visible.
The intended recipient of a parcel, message, or gift.
To take something for granted without checking. The past perfect here identifies an assumption made before the misunderstanding surfaced.
A misunderstanding arising from ambiguity; here, whether “de Clara” identifies the buyer or the gift recipient.
Belonging to someone else; not one's own.
“Would have understood.” Inés imagines how she would have interpreted the same wording in the shopkeeper's position.
String or thin cord used to tie a parcel.
A correction or revision of an earlier statement or understanding.
To linger or take longer; here, to pause rather than leave immediately.

content.title: El paquete de Clara
content.story:
Cuando Inés entró en la tienda, el dependiente estaba sujetando con cinta adhesiva la esquina de una caja. Sobre el mostrador había otra, casi idéntica, con una etiqueta medio oculta bajo el rollo de cinta.

—Vengo por el paquete de Clara —dijo Inés—. Me ha pedido que lo recoja antes de que cierre.

El hombre dejó de trabajar y acercó la caja que acababa de reparar.

—Justo a tiempo. Dígale que la próxima vez procure embalarlo un poco mejor.

Inés examinó la esquina hundida.

—Pues habrá sido durante el transporte. Mi hermana es bastante cuidadosa.

—No digo que no, pero me lo trajo así.

La respuesta le pareció innecesariamente tajante. Clara llevaba toda la semana fuera; difícilmente habría podido llevarle nada a aquella tienda. Sin embargo, Inés dio por sentado que el dependiente se refería al repartidor y prefirió no corregirlo.

—¿Tengo que firmar?

—No. Son ocho euros con cincuenta.

Inés sacó el teléfono, aunque no abrió la aplicación del banco.

—Mi hermana me dijo que ya estaba pagado.

—Puede que lo haya confundido con otro envío.

—Puede —admitió ella, con una sonrisa que no llegó a serlo—. ¿Le importa comprobarlo?

El dependiente soltó un suspiro discreto y consultó una libreta junto a la caja registradora.

—Clara Medina. Una caja para enviar a Zaragoza. Pago pendiente.

—Clara Medina es mi hermana, sí. Pero no vengo a enviar nada.

Él levantó la vista.

—Ha dicho que venía por su paquete.

—Por el que ha llegado a nombre de ella.

Durante unos segundos, ninguno habló. El dependiente miró la caja que había empujado hacia Inés y luego la que seguía bajo el rollo de cinta.

—Ah —dijo, retirándolo.

En la etiqueta de la segunda caja figuraba el nombre de Clara Medina, seguido de la dirección de la tienda y de la indicación «Punto de recogida».

Inés señaló la primera.

—Entonces, ¿esa también es de Clara?

—La dejó el lunes para que la enviáramos. Faltaba confirmar la dirección del destinatario, la persona que debe recibirla. Esta mañana llamó y la confirmó. Como usted ha entrado justo cuando estaba preparándola…

No terminó la frase. Tampoco hacía falta: él había entendido «el paquete que Clara había dejado»; ella, «el paquete que Clara estaba esperando».

—Si hubiera sabido que había dos, habría comprobado la etiqueta antes de pedirle dinero —añadió—. Disculpe el equívoco.

—Yo también podría haber dicho que venía a recoger una entrega —respondió Inés, guardando el teléfono.

El dependiente rectificó la anotación que había empezado a hacer en la libreta y le pidió el código de recogida. Esta vez, antes de entregarle la caja, giró la etiqueta hacia ella.

—Clara Medina. ¿Estamos de acuerdo?

—Ahora sí.

Inés firmó y se acomodó el paquete bajo el brazo. Al llegar a la puerta, miró de nuevo la caja reparada.

—Le diré que el envío sigue aquí.

—Y que ya está bien embalado —contestó él.

Esta vez, la sonrisa de Inés no necesitó ningún esfuerzo.

glossary.meaning: When; introduces the time at which something happens.
To enter. «Entró» narrates a completed past action; «ha entrado» presents it as relevant to the current conversation.
Shop or store.
Shop assistant; the person serving the customer.
To secure or hold something in place. «Estaba sujetando» describes an action in progress in the past.
Adhesive tape used to secure or repair the box.
Corner of the box.
Box containing a parcel.
On top of; locates the box on the counter.
Shop counter where customers are served.
There was or there were. «Había» is impersonal and describes the background situation.
Another or a different one. «Otra» refers to another box; «otro» modifies the masculine noun «envío».
Almost; the boxes look nearly identical.
Identical. «Idéntica» is feminine singular, agreeing with «caja».
Label carrying information about the parcel.
Partly or half, as in partly hidden. Used adverbially, it stays unchanged before feminine «oculta».
Hidden from view. «Oculta» agrees with the feminine noun «etiqueta».
Under or beneath something.
Roll, here of adhesive tape.
To come to collect or get something. «Vengo» is present tense; «venía» reports that purpose from a past viewpoint.
Parcel or package.
To say or tell. «Dijo» narrates past speech, «digo» is present, «Dígale» is a polite command with 'to her', and «diré» is future.
To ask someone to do something or request something. «Ha pedido» links a past request to the present; «pidió» narrates a completed request.
To collect a parcel. «Recoja» is present subjunctive after a request; «recoger» is the infinitive.
Before something happens; followed here by the subjunctive because the shop's closing is still anticipated.
To close the shop. «Cierre» is present subjunctive.
Man; another way of referring to the shop assistant.
To stop doing something; followed by an infinitive.
To work, here repairing and preparing a parcel.
To move something nearer to someone.
To have just done something. «Acababa de reparar» means he had just repaired it at that point in the past.
To repair damage. «Reparada» describes the box as already repaired.
Just in time; before it would have been too late.
Next. «La próxima vez» means on the next occasion.
Occasion or time; used to contrast this encounter with another occasion.
To try or make an effort to do something. «Procure» is a polite command addressed to usted.
To pack or wrap a parcel securely. «Embalarlo» includes 'it'; «embalado» describes the resulting state.
A little; softens the request to pack the parcel better.
Better; describes how the parcel should be packed.
To examine or inspect something closely.
Dented or pushed inward. «Hundida» describes the damaged corner.
Well; introduces Inés's response and her proposed explanation.
It must have been or probably happened. The future perfect expresses a guess about the past, not a future event.
During; places the damage within the period of transport.
Transport or shipping of the parcel.
Sister.
Quite or fairly; indicates a substantial degree of care.
Careful. «Cuidadosa» is feminine singular, describing the sister.
I'm not saying otherwise; concedes the customer's point before introducing a conflicting observation.
But; introduces a contrast or objection.
To bring something to the speaker's location. «Trajo» is a completed past action.
Like that or in that condition; refers to the box being damaged.
Answer or reply.
To seem or strike someone as something. «Le pareció» means it seemed that way to Inés.
Unnecessarily; suggests that the assistant's firmness was not warranted.
Blunt, categorical or overly firm in tone.
To have spent a period in a continuing state. «Llevaba toda la semana fuera» means she had been away all week.
Away or out of town, rather than physically outside the shop.
Hardly or very unlikely; indicates that the suggested action was implausible.
To be able to, or for something to be possible. «Habría podido» refers to a hypothetical past possibility; «Puede» concedes a possibility.
To take something to a destination. «Llevarle» includes 'to him', referring to the assistant.
Anything in negative or negative-like contexts; she could hardly have taken anything, and Inés is not sending anything.
That; points to something viewed as more distant. «Aquella» agrees with «tienda».
However or nevertheless; introduces a contrast with the preceding reasoning.
To take something for granted without checking. «Dio» makes this a completed past assumption.
To refer to or mean someone. «Se refería al» describes what Inés assumed the assistant meant.
Delivery person who brings parcels.
To prefer or choose one course of action over another.
To correct someone or their mistaken statement. «Corregirlo» includes 'him'.
To have to; asks whether an action is required.
To sign, here to acknowledge collection of the parcel.
Eight euros and fifty cents; «con» links the whole currency amount and the cents.
To take something out, here a phone.
Phone.
Although or even though; contrasts taking out the phone with not opening the banking app.
To open, here an application. «Abrió» is preterite.
App, here the bank's mobile application.
Bank or financial institution.
Already; indicates that payment or confirmation was expected to be complete.
Paid. «Estaba pagado» describes the payment as already completed.
It may be that; introduces a possibility and takes the subjunctive.
To mistake one thing for another. «Haya confundido» is perfect subjunctive, referring to a possible earlier mistake.
Shipment or parcel being sent; also the act or service of sending it.
To acknowledge or concede a possibility.
Smile; initially strained or not quite genuine, later effortless.
To actually become or qualify as something. Her expression did not quite amount to a smile; «serlo» refers back to being a smile.
Would you mind…? A polite request followed by an infinitive.
To check or verify. «Comprobarlo» includes 'it'; «habría comprobado» describes what he would have checked in a hypothetical past situation.
To let out a sigh; suggests restrained irritation here.
Subtle or restrained, rather than conspicuous.
To consult or check a written record.
Small notebook used to record parcel details.
Beside or next to.
Cash register or till.
To send or dispatch a parcel. «Enviáramos» is imperfect subjunctive after a past purpose clause.
Payment still outstanding or not yet made.
To look up from what one is reading or doing.
The one that; replaces a repeated noun, here the parcel that has arrived.
To arrive or reach a place. «Ha llegado» refers to the parcel's arrival; «Al llegar» means upon reaching the door.
In someone's name or addressed to that person.
Second as a unit of time. «Unos segundos» means a few seconds.
Neither of the two people; takes a singular verb here.
To speak. «Habló» is preterite.
To look at something.
To push something toward someone. «Había empujado» is pluperfect: the action occurred before this moment in the narrative.
Toward; indicates the direction in which the box or label is moved.
Then or next; marks the sequence of his glances.
To remain or still be somewhere. «Seguía» describes the earlier scene; «sigue» describes the present location.
To remove something. «Retirándolo» is a gerund with 'it', referring to the roll of tape.
Second in a sequence. «Segunda» agrees with «caja».
To appear or be listed on a label or record.
Name, here identifying the person associated with a parcel.
Followed by; describes the order of information on the label.
Address indicating where the parcel is to be delivered.
Written designation or information specifying the shop's role.
Collection point where recipients can pick up parcels.
To point to or indicate something.
First in a sequence. «Primera» refers to the first box, with «caja» understood.
Then or in that case; introduces a conclusion or follow-up question.
That one. «Esa» refers to the box near the assistant.
Also or too.
To belong to or be associated with someone; the ambiguity of this relationship drives the misunderstanding.
To leave or drop something off. «Dejó» narrates the drop-off; «había dejado» places it before another past event.
Monday. With «el», it refers here to a particular past Monday.
So that; introduces a purpose and takes the subjunctive.
To remain to be done. «Faltaba confirmar» means confirmation was still needed.
To confirm or verify the delivery address.
Recipient: the person to whom the parcel is addressed.
Person; used to clarify who the recipient is.
To be supposed or intended to do something; here, the recipient is the person who should receive the parcel.
To receive. «Recibirla» includes 'it', referring to the feminine noun «caja».
This morning; identifies when Clara called.
To call by telephone.
Since or because; introduces the circumstance that explains the assistant's mistaken assumption.
Formal singular 'you'; maintains a polite distance between customer and assistant.
Just as or at precisely the time when.
To prepare the parcel for shipping. «Preparándola» is a gerund with 'it', referring to the box.
To finish; the assistant leaves his explanation unfinished.
Sentence or utterance.
Not … either; adds another negative statement.
To be necessary. «No hacía falta» means it was not necessary.
To understand or interpret. «Había entendido» is pluperfect, identifying an earlier interpretation.
To await or expect a parcel. «Estaba esperando» describes an ongoing expectation in the past.
If I had known; pluperfect subjunctive introduces a past condition that was not fulfilled.
Two; here, two parcels, with the noun omitted.
Before doing something; followed by an infinitive, unlike «antes de que» plus a conjugated verb.
Money; the payment the assistant mistakenly requested.
To add something to what has just been said.
To excuse or forgive. «Disculpe» is a polite command used to apologize.
Misunderstanding caused by an ambiguous expression or mistaken interpretation.
I could have said; conditional perfect acknowledges an alternative wording she did not use.
Delivery; here, the parcel delivered for collection rather than one awaiting dispatch.
To reply or respond.
To put something away. «Guardando» is a gerund describing an accompanying action.
To correct or amend an error, here in a written record.
Written note or entry in the notebook.
To begin doing something. «Había empezado» places the beginning before the correction.
To make or produce, here a written entry.
Collection code used to identify or authorize the parcel pickup.
To hand something over. «Entregarle» includes 'to her'.
To turn something so it faces another direction.
To agree; here, to confirm that both people now identify the same parcel.
Now, yes; implies that the earlier misunderstanding has finally been resolved.
To position something comfortably against one's body. «Se acomodó el paquete» means she settled the parcel securely under her arm.
Arm; the parcel is held under it.
Door or doorway of the shop.
Again; she looks back at the other box once more.
Here, at the shop.
Well or properly; describes the improved packing.
To answer or reply.
To need or require.
No or not any; singular masculine form used before «esfuerzo».
Effort; the final smile is natural rather than forced.

materialIssues: “objeción”, “encargo” and “deshacer el envoltorio” lack useful definitions; the glossary accurately supports selected difficult expressions but only partly meets the learner's request for broad coverage.
strengths: Flexible syntax, past-perfect assumptions and implied interpersonal tension fit the C1 guide well.
All supplied notes give accurate contextual meanings and relevant forms.
The ambiguity of “de Clara” is clearly explained without flattening the characters' reactions.
The parcel misunderstanding resolves while the unwritten gift message creates a natural unresolved thread.

materialIssues: “Procure” is incorrectly described as a polite command addressed to usted. In “Dígale que la próxima vez procure…”, it is present subjunctive in reported instruction, referring to Clara; “Dígale” is the command addressed to Inés.
“podría haber dicho” is incorrectly labeled conditional perfect. It consists of conditional-simple “podría” followed by the perfect infinitive “haber dicho”; the contextual translation is correct.

“Si hubiera sabido que había dos” conflicts with the assistant's apparent awareness of both boxes: both are on his counter, and he has records of Clara's outgoing shipment. Not knowing there were two relevant parcels needs clearer motivation.

“Clara llevaba toda la semana fuera” sits uneasily with “La dejó el lunes”. The timing might be reconcilable, but the narration never revisits Inés's explicit reason for doubting that Clara brought the box.
“Esta vez, la sonrisa de Inés no necesitó ningún esfuerzo” closes the scene without a clearly developed unresolved thread, contrary to the default requirement.
“destinatario, la persona que debe recibirla” is accurate but repeats the glossary definition inside dialogue, making the shopkeeper's explanation slightly instructional.
strengths: Broad definitions cover common vocabulary as requested, alongside idioms, pronoun references and tense distinctions.
“Habrá sido” accurately supports conjecture about the past; “medio oculta” correctly explains invariant adverbial “medio”.
The incoming-versus-outgoing parcel distinction provides a plausible linguistic misunderstanding.
Conjectural future perfect, subjunctive clauses and counterfactual constructions provide appropriate C1 grammatical load.
